slides.headline: The red panda is not a panda.
slides.sub: Not a bear, not a raccoon. It sits in a family of its own

slides.headline: Same name, different animal
slides.body: Red pandas and giant pandas both eat bamboo in Asia's high forests. Despite the shared name, the two species are not closely related.

slides.headline: Raccoon, then bear, then neither
slides.body: Described in 1825 as part of the raccoon family, it was later moved to the bear family. Genetic research now gives it its own.

slides.label: living member of the family Ailuridae
slides.body: The red panda (Ailurus fulgens) is the only living member of its taxonomic family.
slides.source: Smithsonian's National Zoo; IUCN Red List (2015)

slides.headline: It does share the false thumb
slides.body: It has a pseudo-thumb like the giant panda's: a modified wrist bone for grasping bamboo, about 95% of its diet. (Pictured: captive.)

slides.headline: Endangered in the Himalayas
slides.body: It lives at 2,500–4,800 m in India, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar and China. IUCN lists it as Endangered (2015), with numbers decreasing.

slides.headline: Save this for the next panda mix-up.
slides.body: One name, two very different animals. Follow @earthspirit_nature.

caption:
The red panda (Ailurus fulgens) is not a bear, and it is not a close relative of the giant panda either.

Scientists filed it with raccoons in 1825, then with bears, before genetic work placed it alone in the family Ailuridae. It weighs just 3–6.2 kg, and in India it is the official animal of Sikkim. What it does share with the giant panda is a wrist bone that works like a thumb.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.

Source: IUCN Red List (2015); Smithsonian's National Zoo; Britannica; Animal Diversity Web.
